name: Familial Hypomagnesaemia with Hypercalciuria and Nephrocalcinosis

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive tubulopathy caused by loss-of-function variants in CLDN16 (claudin-16/paracellin-1) or CLDN19 (claudin-19), the proteins that build the cation-selective paracellular pore of the thick ascending limb of Henle.
Combined renal magnesium and calcium wasting produces the characteristic triad of hypomagnesaemia, hypercalciuria and bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis.
The CLDN19 subtype adds severe ocular disease - macular colobomata, nystagmus, myopia and visual impairment - whereas CLDN16 disease characteristically spares the eye.
Progressive chronic kidney disease is intrinsic to the disorder and frequently reaches end-stage during adolescence or early adulthood.
Childhood presentation includes recurrent urinary infections, calculi, polyuria and polydipsia, failure to thrive, and tetany or seizures from magnesium depletion.
The fractional excretion of magnesium is inappropriately high for the low serum level, confirming a renal rather than gastrointestinal source of loss.
An incomplete distal acidification defect, hypocitraturia and a raised parathyroid hormone are commonly associated and aggravate stone formation.
Oral magnesium replacement rarely normalises the serum magnesium and does not slow the decline in renal function.
reference.pathophysiology: Claudin-16 and claudin-19 are tight-junction proteins that assemble the selective paracellular pathway of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Here the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage, generated by the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter and apical potassium recycling, normally drives passive reabsorption of magnesium and calcium between the cells. Biallelic loss-of-function variants abolish this cation-selective conductance, so magnesium and calcium escape into the urine, producing renal magnesium wasting and marked hypercalciuria. The sustained high tubular calcium load, compounded by low urinary citrate, precipitates within the medulla as nephrocalcinosis and drives recurrent calcium stone disease. Because claudin-19 is additionally expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium, its loss disrupts ocular development, explaining the eye phenotype confined to that genotype. Ongoing calcium deposition, interstitial inflammation and stone-related obstruction produce chronic tubulointerstitial damage and a relentless loss of glomerular filtration.
additionalDifferentials: Gitelman syndrome, which causes hypomagnesaemia but with hypocalciuria rather than hypercalciuria
Bartter syndrome, with salt wasting, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis but usually preserved magnesium
Hypomagnesaemia with secondary hypocalcaemia due to TRPM6 variants
Autosomal dominant hypomagnesaemia (FXYD2) and HNF1B-related tubulointerstitial disease
Dent disease and other causes of nephrocalcinosis with low-molecular-weight proteinuria
Distal renal tubular acidosis with nephrocalcinosis
Primary hyperparathyroidism or sarcoidosis presenting with hypercalciuria
additionalInvestigations: Serum magnesium paired with the fractional excretion of magnesium to demonstrate renal wasting
Quantified urinary calcium excretion together with urinary citrate
Renal tract ultrasound for medullary nephrocalcinosis and calculi
Parathyroid hormone and markers of glomerular filtration to stage the kidney disease
Formal ophthalmological assessment to detect the CLDN19 ocular phenotype
Assessment of urinary acidification for an incomplete distal tubular acidosis
Molecular testing of CLDN16 and CLDN19
redFlags: Falling glomerular filtration heralding progression toward end-stage kidney disease
Tetany, carpopedal spasm or seizures from severe magnesium depletion
Deteriorating vision or nystagmus suggesting the CLDN19 subtype
Recurrent febrile urinary infections in an infant with failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Renal function declines progressively and many patients reach end-stage kidney disease by early adulthood. Transplantation corrects the tubular transport defect because it is intrinsic to the kidney, although it does not reverse established ocular damage in the CLDN19 subtype.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the disorder as Gitelman syndrome - the presence of hypercalciuria with nephrocalcinosis, rather than hypocalciuria, is the crucial discriminator.
Being falsely reassured by a normal serum calcium, which is typical despite heavy urinary calcium loss.
Expecting magnesium supplementation to correct the biochemistry or protect the kidney, when it reliably does neither.
Overlooking the eyes, so that the CLDN19 subtype and its visual morbidity are missed.
Attributing the nephrocalcinosis to a simple stone diathesis and delaying genetic diagnosis and family screening.
management: Replace ongoing renal magnesium losses with oral magnesium salt supplementation, accepting that full normomagnesaemia is rarely achieved
Reduce hypercalciuria and the stone and nephrocalcinosis burden with thiazide diuretics, generous fluid intake and potassium citrate or alkali to raise urinary citrate
Manage progressive chronic kidney disease with blood-pressure control, RAAS blockade and timely preparation for renal replacement therapy
Treat acute magnesium-depletion complications such as tetany or seizures with parenteral magnesium
Arrange formal ophthalmological assessment and monitoring for the CLDN19 ocular phenotype of macular colobomata, severe myopia and nystagmus
Surveil for and promptly treat urinary tract infection and calculi
Consider kidney transplantation for end-stage disease as it corrects the intrinsic tubular defect, and provide genetic counselling with CLDN16 and CLDN19 family screening
